title: Indian banks seek RBI action as dollar surplus pushes up rupee forward premiums - The HinduBusinessLine
text:
Indian lenders have sought RBI intervention to absorb surplus dollars as rising overnight FX swap rates put upward pressure on rupee forward premiums.

Indian lenders have sought the central bank's intervention in managing a ​dollar surplus that is pushing up overnight FX swap rates ‌and rupee forward premiums, three bankers said.

Foreign investors ​have poured nearly $15 billion into Indian equities ⁠this month, adding to excess dollar liquidity created by previously done sell-buy swaps conducted by the Reserve Bank of India ‌to manage rupee liquidity.

The dollar surplus has driven up overnight dollar/rupee swap rates, which ‌in turn is putting upward pressure on ‌forward premiums, ⁠the bankers, who did not want ⁠to identified since they are not authorised to speak to the media, said.

"The excess dollar liquidity and the market distortions it is ​causing could worsen ‌with month-end approaching, and the situation will become more acute towards the quarter-end," a treasury official at a private sector bank said.

The banks have urged ‌the RBI to conduct buy-sell swaps to mop ​up surplus dollars and rein in the surge in forward premiums, the official added.

The ⁠one-year dollar/rupee forward premium climbed to its highest level since January 2022 on Thursday, rising more than 70 ‌basis points in just 10 days.

Meanwhile, the one-day funding cost jumped to 2 paisas, nearly eight times the level implied by the interest-rate differential between India and the US, the bankers said.

The RBI may be reluctant to intervene because higher forward premiums ‌encourage exporters to hedge while making it more expensive for ​speculators to bet against the rupee, the second banker said.

Both of these, in turn, support ⁠the rupee, in line with the RBI's broader objective ⁠of stabilising the currency, the bankers said. The rupee has staged a sharp recovery to ‌climb to a seven-month high.

The second banker added that the RBI has traditionally preferred to let market ​forces address dollar liquidity imbalances and distortions.
